note.title: Oxidation and reduction (oxygen, hydrogen and electron transfer)

given: Relative atomic masses from the Periodic Table on the Chemistry Data Leaflet

mustKnow: Oxidation: oxygen picked up, hydrogen given away, electrons given away
Reduction: oxygen given away, hydrogen picked up, electrons picked up
Redox = oxidation and reduction in the same reaction
Reducing agent gives electrons and is itself oxidised; oxidising agent takes them and is itself reduced
Half equation method: write the atom and the ion, count the charge, add electrons, check

notOnThisSpec: Oxidation numbers as a formal system

mustBeAbleTo: Give all three definitions of oxidation and all three of reduction, without swapping them
Name the substance oxidised and the substance reduced in a given symbol equation
Define redox with both halves, including 'in the same reaction'
Write a half equation and put the electrons on the side the charges demand (Higher)
Use the molecule, not the atom, when a gas is formed in a half equation (Higher)
Write an ionic equation with the spectator ions left out (Higher)
Name the oxidising agent and the reducing agent, and say what happens to each (Higher)
Explain why the blast furnace and the aluminium cell are redox processes
Calculate a percentage by mass from the Data Leaflet, doubling an Ar where the formula demands
Answer a Name command with a substance, not with a definition
sheet.howExamined: C2, 1 hour 15 minutes: 70 marks at Foundation, 80 at Higher, calculator and Chemistry Data Leaflet allowed. A definition is [1] and CCEA lists three acceptable alternatives for each; the listing rule means writing two of them next to a wrong one earns nothing. A half equation is [3] — reactant and product with an arrow, electrons on the correct side, correct balancing — and each mark depends on the one before it, so a wrong formula costs all three. 'Which species is oxidised' is [1] and wants the substance named.
traps: Electrons on the wrong side of a half equation (Summer 2025 C2 H Q2(b)(v))
The wrong number of electrons for the charge on the ion (Summer 2025 C2 H Q2(b)(v))
A half equation written for the atom instead of the molecule (Summer 2024 C2 H Q3(e))
Giving the definition of oxidation when reduction was asked (Summer 2024 C2 F Q2)
Saying 'both reduction and oxidation' but leaving out 'in the same reaction' (Summer 2024 C2 F Q3(b))
Reciting definitions instead of naming which substance did which (Summer 2023 C2 H Q2(c))
Spectator ions written into an ionic equation (Summer 2024 C2 H Q2(c))
Swapping the two agents, because each is named for its effect on the other substance
Calling a reduction combustion or the Haber process (Summer 2024 C2 H Q2)

workedExamples.stem:
Magnesium powder is heated with copper(II) oxide:
$\ce{Mg + CuO -> MgO + Cu}$
(a) Name the substance that is oxidised, and say how you know. [2]
(b) Name the substance that is reduced, and say how you know. [2]

steps.working: Follow the oxygen. On the left it is attached to the copper; on the right it is attached to the magnesium.
steps.decision: Track one atom, not the whole equation. Oxygen is the thing that moved, so oxygen is the thing to follow.

steps.working: The magnesium has gained oxygen, so the magnesium is oxidised.
steps.decision: Name the substance first, then the reason. A definition on its own answers a different question.

options: Because the mark is for identifying the substance, not for reciting the definition
Because magnesium is more reactive than copper
Because oxidation always happens to the metal on the left
whyMenu.explain: Summer 2023's report records candidates giving the general definitions correctly but not saying which substance had undergone each process.

steps.working: The copper(II) oxide has lost its oxygen, so the copper(II) oxide is reduced.
steps.decision: Name the compound that lost it, not the element left behind. It is the copper oxide that is reduced; the copper is what reduction produced.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) The magnesium is oxidised, because it has gained oxygen. (b) The copper(II) oxide is reduced, because it has lost its oxygen.

twin.stem: In $\ce{Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2}$, name the substance that is reduced and say how you know.

accepted: the iron(III) oxide is reduced because it has lost oxygen

workedExamples.stem:
Zinc is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution. The ionic equation is $\ce{Zn + Cu^{2+} -> Zn^{2+} + Cu}$.
(a) Write the half equation for the change undergone by the zinc. [3]
(b) Write the half equation for the change undergone by the copper(II) ions. [3]
Write a charge with the superscript sign — Zn²⁺ or Zn2⁺ — and an electron as e⁻.

steps.working: Zinc starts as an atom and finishes as a 2+ ion: Zn → Zn^2+.
steps.decision: Take one species at a time and write only what happens to it. A half equation has one element on each side, never the whole reaction.

steps.working: Charges: 0 on the left, +2 on the right. Two electrons are missing, and they were lost, so they go on the right: Zn → Zn^2+ + 2e^-.
steps.decision: Electrons go on the side that makes the two totals equal. Lost electrons appear with the products; gained electrons appear with the reactants.

options: Because the two sides of any equation must carry the same total charge
Because electrons are always written on the right
Because zinc is a metal, and metals always end up positive
whyMenu.explain: Charge is conserved just as atoms are. Summer 2025's report names electrons on the wrong side as a main fault here.

steps.working: Copper starts as a 2+ ion and finishes as an atom: Cu^2+ → Cu.
steps.decision: Same method, opposite direction. The ion is on the left this time because that is where it starts.

steps.working: Charges: +2 on the left, 0 on the right. Two electrons must be added on the left: Cu^2+ + 2e^- → Cu.
steps.decision: Gained electrons go in with the reactants. Check the totals: +2 − 2 = 0 on the left, 0 on the right.

twin.stem: Write the half equation for a magnesium atom becoming a magnesium ion. Write a charge with the superscript sign — Zn²⁺ or Zn2⁺ — and an electron as e⁻.

workedExamples.stem:
In the blast furnace, $\ce{Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2}$.
(a) Name the reducing agent and explain your choice. [2]
(b) Name the oxidising agent and explain your choice. [2]

figure.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox="0 0 700 296" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="cagt"><title id="cagt">Two labelled boxes, the reducing agent on the left and the oxidising agent on the right, joined by an arrow that carries two electrons from left to right</title><defs><marker id="cag" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.7"><rect x="40" y="90" width="270" height="110" rx="8"/><rect x="390" y="90" width="270" height="110" rx="8"/></g><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4"><path d="M318 134 H382" marker-end="url(%23cag)"/></g><g fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="1" stroke="none"><circle cx="336" cy="116" r="5"/><circle cx="356" cy="116" r="5"/></g><g font-family="inherit" font-size="13" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle"><text x="175" y="126" font-size="15" font-weight="600">reducing agent</text><text x="175" y="154">gives electrons away</text><text x="175" y="180">so it is changed itself</text><text x="525" y="126" font-size="15" font-weight="600">oxidising agent</text><text x="525" y="154">takes electrons</text><text x="525" y="180">so it is changed itself</text><text x="350" y="104" font-size="11.5">electrons</text></g><g font-family="inherit" font-size="12.5" fill="currentColor"><text x="24" y="34" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Which one is the agent?</text><text x="24" y="54" font-size="11.5">The two filled circles on the arrow are electrons moving from left to right.</text><text x="24" y="240" font-size="11.5">Decide first what happened to each substance; the two job titles follow from that.</text></g></svg>
figure.alt: Two labelled boxes, the reducing agent on the left and the oxidising agent on the right, joined by an arrow that carries two electrons from left to right.

steps.working: Work out who was reduced first: the iron(III) oxide lost its oxygen, so it was reduced.
steps.decision: You cannot name an agent until you know what happened to each substance. Do the reduction and oxidation first, the job titles second.

steps.working: Something must have taken that oxygen: the carbon monoxide, which became carbon dioxide. So the carbon monoxide was oxidised.
steps.decision: Oxygen is conserved, so a loss on one side is always a gain on the other. This is the check that stops you naming the same substance twice.

steps.working: The reducing agent is the one that did the reducing: carbon monoxide. It reduced the iron(III) oxide by taking its oxygen, and was oxidised itself.
steps.decision: Read the name as a job title, not as a description of what happened to it. The reducing agent is always the substance that is itself oxidised.

options: Because an agent is named for what it does to the other substance
Because the reducing agent is always the one that is reduced
Because the reducing agent is always a gas
whyMenu.explain: The naming is about the effect on the partner. The reducing agent reduces something else and is oxidised in doing it.

steps.working: The oxidising agent is the iron(III) oxide: it oxidised the carbon monoxide by giving up its oxygen, and was reduced itself.
steps.decision: The two answers are always the two substances, one each way round. If you name the same one twice, something has gone wrong.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) Carbon monoxide is the reducing agent: it removes the oxygen from the iron(III) oxide, reducing it, and is itself oxidised to carbon dioxide. (b) Iron(III) oxide is the oxidising agent: it gives its oxygen to the carbon monoxide, oxidising it, and is itself reduced to iron.

twin.stem: In $\ce{2Al + Fe2O3 -> 2Fe + Al2O3}$, name the reducing agent and explain your choice.

accepted: aluminium, because it takes the oxygen from the iron(III) oxide and is oxidised itself

items.stem: A magnesium atom loses two electrons. What is the charge on the ion it becomes?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 §1.2 — charge on a simple ion; you are not expected to have met redox yet

options.feedback: Losing two negative charges leaves the ion two positive. That single idea is the whole of the Higher half of this lesson.
Losing negative charge makes an ion more positive, not more negative. Section 3 of the lesson leans on this, so it is worth fixing now.
An atom is neutral because its protons and electrons balance. Take electrons away and the protons win.

items.stem: In $\ce{Fe2O3}$, which element is joined to the oxygen?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 §1.5 — reading a formula

options.feedback: Fe is iron, and Fe₂O₃ is iron(III) oxide. Most of this lesson follows the oxygen on and off that compound.
Fluorine is F on its own; Fe is iron. Symbols are case-sensitive and the second letter matters.
There is no hydrogen in this formula. Fe is iron and O is oxygen.

items.stem: Which particle in an atom carries a negative charge?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 §1.1 — the three sub-atomic particles

options.feedback: Electrons are the negative ones, and they are the currency the whole of this topic is traded in.
Protons are positive. Electrons are the negative particles, and they are what moves in a redox reaction.
Neutrons carry no charge at all. The negative particle is the electron.

items.stem: In $\ce{CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O}$, which substance is oxidised?
items.skill: Identify the oxidised species from an equation

options.feedback: The hydrogen gains oxygen and becomes water, so it is oxidised.
The copper(II) oxide loses its oxygen, which is reduction. Follow the oxygen: whoever ends up with it is the one oxidised.
The copper is a product, and it has less oxygen than it started with, not more.
The water is the product of the oxidation, not the substance that was oxidised. Name the starting substance.

items.stem: Which of these is a definition of reduction that CCEA accepts?

figure.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox="0 0 700 302" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="coilt"><title id="coilt">A table of the three ways oxidation and reduction are defined: oxygen gained or lost, hydrogen lost or gained, and electrons lost or gained</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4"><path d="M50 54 H640"/><path d="M50 96 H640"/><path d="M50 138 H640"/><path d="M50 180 H640"/><path d="M50 222 H640"/><path d="M50 54 V222"/><path d="M280 54 V222"/><path d="M460 54 V222"/><path d="M640 54 V222"/></g><g font-family="inherit" font-size="13" fill="currentColor"><text x="62" y="82" font-weight="600">What changes</text><text x="292" y="82" font-weight="600">Oxidation</text><text x="472" y="82" font-weight="600">Reduction</text><text x="62" y="124">oxygen</text><text x="292" y="124">gained</text><text x="472" y="124">lost</text><text x="62" y="166">hydrogen</text><text x="292" y="166">lost</text><text x="472" y="166">gained</text><text x="62" y="208">electrons (Higher Tier)</text><text x="292" y="208">lost</text><text x="472" y="208">gained</text><text x="50" y="36" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Three ways to spot oxidation and reduction</text><text x="50" y="56" font-size="11.5">Read a row across: what oxidation does to that thing, reduction does the opposite.</text><text x="50" y="256" font-size="12">OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons, Reduction Is Gain of electrons.</text><text x="50" y="280" font-size="12">Both happen together in the same reaction, which is why it is called redox.</text></g></svg>

options.feedback: Any one of gain of electrons, gain of hydrogen or loss of oxygen earns the mark.
That is oxidation. OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain. Summer 2024 examiners recorded candidates giving the oxidation definition when reduction was asked.
Gaining oxygen is oxidation. Reduction loses oxygen and gains hydrogen or electrons.
Losing hydrogen is oxidation. Read the table row by row: whatever oxidation does, reduction does the opposite.

items.stem: What does the word redox mean?

options.text: oxidation and reduction happening in the same reaction
options.feedback: Both halves, and the words 'in the same reaction' — that second half is a mark of its own.
Summer 2024 examiners recorded most candidates getting this far and no further. Say as well that the two run together, inside one reaction.

options.text: a reaction that gives out heat
options.feedback: That is an exothermic reaction, which is a different idea. Redox is about electrons or oxygen changing hands.

options.text: a reaction that can go both ways
options.feedback: That is a reversible reaction. Redox means reduction and oxidation together.

items.skill: Put the electrons on the correct side

options.feedback: Three electrons are lost, so they leave with the products and the charges cancel: 0 on the left, +3 and −3 on the right.
The electrons are on the wrong side. That would make the left −3 and the right +3. Summer 2025 examiners named this as a main fault on this very question.
The number of electrons must match the charge: an iron(III) ion is 3+, so three electrons are lost.
That is written backwards, and the electrons are on the wrong side for it too. The question starts from the atom.

items.stem: Bromide ions are oxidised at the anode during electrolysis. Which half equation is correct?
items.skill: Use the molecule, not the atom, in a half equation

options.feedback: Bromine leaves as a molecule, so two bromide ions are needed and two electrons are released.
Bromine is diatomic: the product is Br₂, not a lone Br atom. Summer 2024 examiners recorded exactly this fault with oxygen at the anode.
Oxidation loses electrons, so they belong on the right; and the bromines do not balance.
The bromines balance, but the electrons are on the wrong side for an oxidation.

items.stem: Magnesium is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution: $\ce{Mg + Cu^{2+} -> Mg^{2+} + Cu}$. Which species is the reducing agent?
items.skill: Name the agent rather than the process

options.feedback: It gives its electrons away, reducing the copper(II) ions, and is oxidised itself.
They take electrons, so they oxidise the magnesium: they are the oxidising agent. An agent is named for what it does to the other substance.
The sulfate ions are spectators: they are unchanged on both sides and take no part.
The copper is a product. The agents are the two substances you start with.

indicativeContent.point: each magnesium atom loses two electrons
loss of electrons is oxidation, so the magnesium is oxidised
each copper(II) ion gains two electrons
gain of electrons is reduction, so the copper(II) ions are reduced
the half equations are Mg → Mg2+ + 2e− and Cu2+ + 2e− → Cu
the magnesium is the reducing agent and the copper(II) ions are the oxidising agent

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Take the two species one at a time, and say for each what it did with its electrons.
Name the substances. Summer 2023's report records answers that gave the definitions but never said which substance did which.
Finish with the two agent names and the phrase 'in the same reaction'.
parts.workedSolution: Each magnesium atom loses two electrons and becomes a magnesium ion, and loss of electrons is oxidation, so the magnesium is oxidised: Mg → Mg2+ + 2e−. Each copper(II) ion gains those two electrons and becomes a copper atom, and gain of electrons is reduction, so the copper(II) ions are reduced: Cu2+ + 2e− → Cu. Because the magnesium gives its electrons away it reduces the copper(II) ions, so the magnesium is the reducing agent; because the copper(II) ions take electrons they oxidise the magnesium, so they are the oxidising agent. Oxidation and reduction are happening in the same reaction, which is what the word redox means. The sulfate ions are spectators: they are unchanged throughout and take no part.

findTheMistake.stem:
Ciara is asked: 'Write the half equation for the change from an iron atom to an iron(III) ion. [3]'
Her answer:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 2 and 3 are exactly right, and they contradict line 1. If the iron loses three electrons, those electrons leave with the products, so they belong on the right-hand side. As written, the left side carries −3 and the right side +3, which cannot be an equation. Summer 2025 examiners named electrons on the incorrect side as one of the two commonest faults on this very question.
findTheMistake.feedback: One of the three marks: the reactant and product with an arrow are right. The electron mark goes because they are on the wrong side, and because the balancing mark depends on the electron mark, that one goes with it. Use the charge check every time: 0 on the left, +3 and −3 on the right, which is 0.

findTheMistake.stem:
Ruairí is asked: 'In $\ce{Mg + CuO -> MgO + Cu}$, name the substance that is reduced and explain your answer. [2]'
His answer:
studentWorking: The copper(II) oxide has lost its oxygen.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The answer contradicts its own evidence. Lines 2 and 3 are both right, and together they point straight at the copper(II) oxide: it is the substance that lost oxygen, and losing oxygen is reduction. Line 1 names the other substance. The magnesium gained that oxygen, so the magnesium is oxidised. Summer 2023's report describes exactly this — candidates who could give the general definitions but could not state which substance had undergone each process.
findTheMistake.feedback: One of the two marks: the reason is right, and it is doing the work for you. Read your own last two lines back before you name the substance — whichever one lost the oxygen is the one that was reduced. A quick habit: underline the command word first, and if it says Name, make the first word of your answer a name.

findTheMistake.stem:
Tomás is asked: 'Zinc is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution. Write the ionic equation. [2]'
His answer:
studentWorking: Zn + Cu2+ + SO4 2- → Zn2+ + SO4 2- + Cu
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The chemistry underneath is right, but an ionic equation leaves out the ions that do not change. The sulfate ion appears unchanged on both sides, so it is a spectator and should not be written at all. Summer 2024 examiners recorded candidates including additional ions in exactly this equation.
findTheMistake.feedback: Partial credit: the species that do change are all correct and on the right sides. What costs the second mark is the sulfate. Before you write an ionic equation, cross out anything that is identical on both sides — whatever is left is the equation.

prompts.prompt: Give the three definitions of oxidation.
prompts.answer: Gaining oxygen. Losing hydrogen. Losing electrons.

prompts.prompt: Give the three definitions of reduction.
prompts.answer: Loss of oxygen; gain of hydrogen; gain of electrons.

prompts.prompt: What does redox mean? Both halves of the answer, please.
prompts.answer: Oxidation and reduction taking place in the same reaction.

prompts.prompt: In $\ce{CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O}$, which substance is oxidised, which is reduced, and how do you know?
prompts.answer: The hydrogen is oxidised because it gains oxygen; the copper(II) oxide is reduced because it loses oxygen.
Oxidation Is Loss of electrons, Reduction Is Gain of electrons.

prompts.prompt: Write the half equation for an iron atom becoming an iron(III) ion, and say which side the electrons go on and why.
prompts.answer: Fe → Fe3+ + 3e-. The electrons are lost, so they go on the right, and the charges then match: 0 on the left, +3 − 3 = 0 on the right.

prompts.prompt: Write the half equation for a copper(II) ion becoming a copper atom.
prompts.answer: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu. The electrons are gained, so they go in with the reactants.

prompts.prompt: What is a reducing agent, and what happens to it?
prompts.answer: The substance that reduces something else, by giving electrons away or taking oxygen off it. It is itself oxidised.

prompts.prompt: Name the reducing agent in the blast furnace and say what it does.
prompts.answer: Carbon monoxide. It takes the oxygen from the iron(III) oxide, reducing it to iron, and is itself oxidised to carbon dioxide.

prompts.prompt: In $\ce{Zn + Cu^{2+} -> Zn^{2+} + Cu}$, name the species oxidised, the species reduced, and the two agents.
prompts.answer: The zinc is oxidised (it loses two electrons) and is the reducing agent. The copper(II) ions are reduced (they gain two electrons) and are the oxidising agent.

findings.asked: Write the half equation showing an iron atom forming an iron(III) ion.
findings.wentWrong: The part was a strong discriminator: the electrons were often placed on the wrong side of the arrow, or the wrong number of them was used.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Wrote Fe on the left and Fe3+ on the right, then added exactly three electrons to the right so that both sides carried the same total charge.
findings.rule: Write the atom and the ion first, count the charge on each side, then put in as many electrons as it takes to make the two totals equal.

findings.asked: Write the half equation for what happens at the positive electrode during electrolysis.
findings.wentWrong: It was answered well by only a few: the commonest fault was writing the equation for the oxygen atom instead of the oxygen molecule.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Started from the diatomic molecule and balanced the electrons to it. The marks run in a fixed order — species and arrow, the side the electrons sit on, the balancing — and each is gated by the one above it.
findings.rule: Gases leave as molecules. Write O2, Cl2 or Br2 first, then balance the ions and the electrons to that.

findings.asked: Explain, in terms of electrons, why the thermite reaction is described as a redox reaction (the 6-mark writing question).
findings.wentWrong: The answers drifted into generalities: both definitions were there, but neither was pinned to a substance in the reaction on the page.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Named the substance each time — the aluminium atoms lose electrons and are oxidised, the iron ions gain them and are reduced — before adding that both happen in the same reaction.
findings.rule: Start every sentence with the substance, then the process, then the evidence. A definition with no substance in it answers a different question.

findings.asked: State what is meant by a redox reaction.
findings.wentWrong: Most candidates reached the first mark by saying that both reduction and oxidation take place, then stopped short of the second: that the two happen together, inside one reaction.
findings.rule: Two marks means two ideas. 'Oxidation and reduction' is the first; 'in the same reaction' is the second, and it is four words long.

findings.asked: Write the ionic equation for a displacement reaction.
findings.wentWrong: The ionic equation defeated a large share of the entry, and the commonest fault was leaving in ions that take no part in the change.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Crossed out every ion that appeared unchanged on both sides and wrote only what was left.
findings.rule: An ionic equation contains only the species that change. Anything identical on both sides is a spectator and is not written.

findings.asked: Identify a given reaction as a reduction.
findings.wentWrong: Few candidates answered it: the commonest responses gave the definition of oxidation instead, or stated that the magnesium oxide had been oxidised. Elsewhere the reaction was called combustion or the Haber process.
findings.rule: Decide what happened to the oxygen before you reach for a name. A substance that ends with less oxygen than it started with has been reduced.

insight.ruleToRemember: Name the substance, then say what happened to it, then give the evidence. Every mark in this topic is lost by answering with a definition where a substance was asked for, or by putting the electrons on the side that feels right instead of the side the charges demand.
insight.aStarSignal: The agent names. A candidate who can say that the magnesium is the reducing agent because it gives its electrons away, and is therefore itself oxidised, has understood the whole topic rather than memorised OIL RIG.
